S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every confirmed thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, or thermal injury to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, including incidents initially reported by customers or service personnel. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk to their unit or household, and provide follow-up instructions promptly.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every confirmed thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, or thermal injury to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, including incidents initially reported by customers or service personnel. A preliminary report may be followed by a corrected or complete report within 10 business days. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk to their unit or household, and provide follow-up instructions promptly. Records of all incidents, including those not initially reportable, must be retained and reconciled in periodic reports to regulators.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol before sale and after a material design change. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% for any model. Manufacturers must provide per-model results and test methods to regulators and disclose the per-model failure rate and a clear safety summary to customers purchasing that model; results must not be publicly published by company or model.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol before sale and after a material design change. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% for any model. Manufacturers must provide per-model results and test methods to regulators and disclose the per-model failure rate and a clear safety summary to customers purchasing that model; results must not be publicly published by company or model. If a model exceeds the limit, its manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator, submit a corrective-action plan, and retest within a regulator-set period. Regulators may restrict sales if corrective action is inadequate or testing identifies an imminent serious risk; exceeding the test limit alone does not automatically ban a model. Manufacturers must retain test records and provide affected customers with safety instructions if testing identifies a material risk.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off no later than 12 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must retrofit or otherwise enable remote shut-off for installed units within 6 years after adoption, where technically feasible, and provide customers clear instructions for requesting or using shut-off.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off no later than 12 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must retrofit or otherwise enable remote shut-off for installed units within 6 years after adoption, where technically feasible, and provide customers clear instructions for requesting or using shut-off. Shut-off must not replace emergency services or other required safety protections; activation and access controls must be documented and tested.

parameters.quote: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers, and a regulator-supervised recall of that model is mandatory. The regulator shall determine the appropriate scope and remedy, which may include repair, replacement, or refund.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers, and a regulator-supervised recall of that model is mandatory. The regulator shall determine the appropriate scope and remedy, which may include repair, replacement, or refund.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Before purchase, customers must receive clear safety notices describing material known risks, relevant safety instructions, and the model’s 55 °C sustained-heat test results. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of newly identified material risks and provide protective instructions. When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers, and a regulator-supervised recall of that model is mandatory. The regulator shall determine the appropriate scope and remedy, which may include repair, replacement, or refund. A recall does not itself constitute an automatic market ban; regulators may separately restrict sales based on the risk and adequacy of corrective action. Recall notices must explain the risk and provide repair, replacement, or refund instructions.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C test
ground_truth_claims.message_text: For the evidence base, Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C test and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year. Northwind’s company-wide rate was 8.6 per 100,000; 3 thermal incidents were not reported to a regulator. These figures make the current 5% limit and automatic 8/100,000 recall trigger consequential for our products. We should use regulator-supervised corrective action and risk review rather than treating either threshold as an automatic market ban or recall.

judge_section_notes: S1 requires reporting all confirmed incidents within 24h and customer notice within 72h, but limits scope to confirmed incidents. S2 sets a 5% failure limit at 55°C with per-model disclosure to customers and regulators, but exceeding the limit does not automatically stop sales, leaving it to regulator discretion. S3 mandates new-unit shut-off within 12 months and retrofit within 6 years where feasible, with no alternative required. S4 requires built-in fire suppression within 36 months. S5 mandates recall above 8/100k with prompt notices, but lacks a serious-injury recall clause.
